nameStory: The castor bean gets its name from the Latin word 'ricinus,' meaning tick, because the mottled seeds were thought to resemble these blood-sucking parasites. Despite being called a 'bean,' it's not actually related to true beans at all – it's a member of the spurge family, making this name quite misleading!
description: Castor bean is a fast-growing tropical plant that's occasionally grown as an ornamental in New England gardens. This dramatic plant can reach 6-10 feet tall in a single growing season, with large, palm-shaped leaves that can span a foot across. The plant produces clusters of spiky seed pods that split open to reveal large, beautifully patterned seeds that look like oversized ticks.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, glossy leaves shaped like giant hands with 5-11 pointed lobes radiating from the center. They feel smooth and waxy to the touch, often with reddish stems and veins.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Large, bean-like seeds with striking mottled patterns in brown, black, and tan – they're often described as looking like fancy marbles or ticks. Handle with extreme caution as they're highly toxic.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Fast-growing, upright plant with thick, hollow stems that can reach impressive heights in one season. The whole plant has a tropical, exotic appearance that stands out in temperate gardens.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, inconspicuous flowers arranged in tall spikes, with female flowers at the top (reddish) and male flowers below (yellowish). No petals – just clusters of reproductive parts.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Spiky, round seed pods about the size of a walnut that start green and turn brown. They split into three sections with a satisfying 'pop' when ripe, often launching seeds several feet away.

habitat: In New England, castor bean is found almost exclusively in cultivated gardens and occasionally as an escape near old homesteads or compost piles. It thrives in rich, well-drained soil in full sun and warm, protected locations. Since it's tropical, it cannot survive New England winters and is grown as an annual ornamental.

seasonality.spring: Seeds are planted after all danger of frost has passed, usually late May or early June in New England. Young plants emerge with their first rounded seed leaves before developing the characteristic palmate foliage.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when the dramatic foliage is most impressive and flowers appear in tall spikes. Seeds begin forming in spiky pods by late summer.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods ripen and split open with audible pops, scattering the beautiful but deadly seeds. Plants are killed by the first frost, turning brown and collapsing.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground presence in New England – the entire plant dies with frost. Only scattered seeds remain, which cannot survive the cold winter.

funFact: The seeds contain ricin, one of the most deadly natural toxins known – just one seed can be lethal to a child, and three to an adult, yet the same plant produces castor oil, a common medicine and industrial lubricant used safely for centuries!
confusionNotes: The large, palmate leaves might be confused with Japanese aralia or fatsia, but castor bean's leaves are much more deeply lobed and the plant grows much taller. The spiky seed pods are unique and unmistakable once you see them.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name, castor 'beans' aren't beans at all – true beans belong to the legume family, while this plant is in the spurge family along with poinsettias and rubber trees. The beautiful seeds are extremely dangerous and should never be handled by children or put in the mouth.
compareHints: Castor bean is the only species in its genus Ricinus, making it unique. Within the spurge family, it's easily distinguished from other members like poinsettia or spurge weeds by its massive size, palmate leaves, and large toxic seeds. Most other spurges in New England are small weedy plants with tiny flowers and milky sap.
